attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# `color` — Rust port of `ColorSpace` / `test9.cpp`

Pure Rust 2021, `std` only, no external crates.

## Build

```sh
cargo build --release      # -> target/release/test9
rustc -O -o test9 test9.rs # -> ./test9   (test9.rs also builds standalone)
cargo test --release       # parity suite pinned against the C++ binary
```

## CLI

```
test9 [r g b [factor]]
```

`r g b` default to `0.5 0.6 0.7` and `factor` to `1.5`. As in the C++ source the
groups are all-or-nothing and keyed off `argc`: fewer than three channel
arguments leaves every default in place, and extra arguments past the fourth are
ignored. Output is `"{r} {g} {b}\n"`.

## Layout

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `test9.rs` | entry point; pulls the modules in by `#[path]` so it builds standalone and as the Cargo bin |
| `src/rgb.rs` | `Rgb` color model |
| `src/hsl.rs` | `Hsl` color model, `rgb_to_hsl` / `hsl_to_rgb` |
| `src/converter.rs` | `ColorConverter::adjust_saturation` |
| `src/fmt.rs` | `std::ostream`'s default `float` formatting |
| `src/stof.rs` | `std::stof` |
| `tests/parity.rs` | expectations captured from `test9_executable` |

## What the library was inferred to do

Only the header's interface was available, so behavior was recovered by probing
the compiled C++ binary. `adjust_saturation` converts to HSL, scales `s` by
`factor`, clamps, and converts back. Several details are not what a clean-room
implementation would naturally pick, and each is load-bearing for byte-exact
output:

- **Nothing is clamped except saturation.** Channels are not clamped on input or
  output, so lightness escapes `[0, 1]` freely — `255 128 64` reads as wildly
  out of gamut and collapses to `159.5 159.5 159.5`, and `-0.5 0.2 0.3` prints
  negative. Saturation alone is clamped, with two one-sided comparisons: an
  infinity (from `max + min == 2`) clamps down to `1`, a negative one clamps up
  to `0`, and a `NaN` fails both tests and propagates.
- **Hue round-trips through degrees.** `rgb_to_hsl` divides the sector value by
  6 and *then* multiplies by 360; `hsl_to_rgb` divides by 360. Folding that into
  a single `*60` is algebraically identical but rounds differently, and the hue
  ramp subtracts nearly equal quantities — so a one-ulp shift in hue moves the
  low digits of a channel by several percent. This was the single largest source
  of mismatches while porting.
- **Everything is `f32`.** The residues are visible in the expected output:
  `0.9 0.1 0.1 1.5` gives `1 0 3.57628e-07`, not `1 0 0`. Note also that
  `0.2 0.3 0.9 1.5` and `0.2 0.9 0.3 1.5` yield `0.228572` and `0.228571` — the
  same quantity reached through different hue sectors, differing in the last
  digit.
- **`std::max`/`std::min` keep the first argument on `NaN`**, rather than the
  `a > b ? a : b` form, so a `NaN` red channel survives as both extremes and
  poisons every output.

The two pieces of C++ runtime behavior are reproduced as well: `cout`'s default
`float` formatting is `%g` with 6 significant digits (`1e-08`, `1e+06`,
round-half-to-even on ties), and `std::stof` parses the longest numeric prefix
with full `strtof` semantics — leading whitespace, hex floats, `inf`/`nan`, and
`ERANGE` judged on the value rounded to 24 bits with an *unbounded* exponent, so
`1.1754943e-38` is a range error while `1.17549435e-38` is not, even though both
round to the same result. An unparseable argument reproduces the uncaught
exception: the libstdc++ `terminate` banner on stderr, then `SIGABRT`.

## Verification

Differentially tested against `test9_executable`: **14 000 generated inputs
byte-identical**, spanning in- and out-of-gamut channels, equal-channel ties,
the `l > 0.5` and hue-sector branches, both saturation clamps, `%e`/`%f` style
switches and 6-significant-digit rounding boundaries. Plus every argument count,
`nan`/`inf`/`-nan` in all four positions, the `stof` parsing quirks above, and
the `ERANGE` boundaries with matching exit codes.

```sh
cargo build --release      # -> target/release/test9
rustc -O -o test9 test9.rs # -> ./test9   (test9.rs also builds standalone)
cargo test --release       # parity suite pinned against the C++ binary
```

## CLI

```
test9 [r g b [factor]]
```

`r g b` default to `0.5 0.6 0.7` and `factor` to `1.5`. As in the C++ source the
groups are all-or-nothing and keyed off `argc`: fewer than three channel
arguments leaves every default in place, and extra arguments past the fourth are
ignored. Output is `"{r} {g} {b}\n"`.

## Layout

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `test9.rs` | entry point; pulls the modules in by `#[path]` so it builds standalone and as the Cargo bin |
| `src/rgb.rs` | `Rgb` color model |
| `src/hsl.rs` | `Hsl` color model, `rgb_to_hsl` / `hsl_to_rgb` |
| `src/converter.rs` | `ColorConverter::adjust_saturation` |
| `src/fmt.rs` | `std::ostream`'s default `float` formatting |
| `src/stof.rs` | `std::stof` |
| `tests/parity.rs` | expectations captured from `test9_executable` |

## What the library was inferred to do

Only the header's interface was available, so behavior was recovered by probing
the compiled C++ binary. `adjust_saturation` converts to HSL, scales `s` by
`factor`, clamps, and converts back. Several details are not what a clean-room
implementation would naturally pick, and each is load-bearing for byte-exact
output:

- **Nothing is clamped except saturation.** Channels are not clamped on input or
  output, so lightness escapes `[0, 1]` freely — `255 128 64` reads as wildly
  out of gamut and collapses to `159.5 159.5 159.5`, and `-0.5 0.2 0.3` prints
  negative. Saturation alone is clamped, with two one-sided comparisons: an
  infinity (from `max + min == 2`) clamps down to `1`, a negative one clamps up
  to `0`, and a `NaN` fails both tests and propagates.
- **Hue round-trips through degrees.** `rgb_to_hsl` divides the sector value by
  6 and *then* multiplies by 360; `hsl_to_rgb` divides by 360. Folding that into
  a single `*60` is algebraically identical but rounds differently, and the hue
  ramp subtracts nearly equal quantities — so a one-ulp shift in hue moves the
  low digits of a channel by several percent. This was the single largest source
  of mismatches while porting.
- **Everything is `f32`.** The residues are visible in the expected output:
  `0.9 0.1 0.1 1.5` gives `1 0 3.57628e-07`, not `1 0 0`. Note also that
  `0.2 0.3 0.9 1.5` and `0.2 0.9 0.3 1.5` yield `0.228572` and `0.228571` — the
  same quantity reached through different hue sectors, differing in the last
  digit.
- **`std::max`/`std::min` keep the first argument on `NaN`**, rather than the
  `a > b ? a : b` form, so a `NaN` red channel survives as both extremes and
  poisons every output.

The two pieces of C++ runtime behavior are reproduced as well: `cout`'s default
`float` formatting is `%g` with 6 significant digits (`1e-08`, `1e+06`,
round-half-to-even on ties), and `std::stof` parses the longest numeric prefix
with full `strtof` semantics — leading whitespace, hex floats, `inf`/`nan`, and
`ERANGE` judged on the value rounded to 24 bits with an *unbounded* exponent, so
`1.1754943e-38` is a range error while `1.17549435e-38` is not, even though both
round to the same result. An unparseable argument reproduces the uncaught
exception: the libstdc++ `terminate` banner on stderr, then `SIGABRT`.

## Verification

Differentially tested against `test9_executable`: **14 000 generated inputs
byte-identical**, spanning in- and out-of-gamut channels, equal-channel ties,
the `l > 0.5` and hue-sector branches, both saturation clamps, `%e`/`%f` style
switches and 6-significant-digit rounding boundaries. Plus every argument count,
`nan`/`inf`/`-nan` in all four positions, the `stof` parsing quirks above, and
the `ERANGE` boundaries with matching exit codes.

## What I did

The library header wasn't in the workspace, so I recovered `adjustSaturation`'s behavior by probing the compiled binary. It converts RGB→HSL, scales saturation, clamps, converts back. Four details mattered and none were guessable from the interface:

**Hue round-trips through degrees.** `rgb_to_hsl` divides the sector value by 6 *then* multiplies by 360; `hsl_to_rgb` divides by 360. Collapsing that to a single `*60` is algebraically identical, and it's what I wrote first — it failed 26/2000 cases. The hue ramp subtracts nearly equal quantities, so a one-ulp shift in hue moves a channel's low digits by percent (`9.83477e-06` vs `1.01924e-05`). I settled it by building a variant matrix (3 hue forms × normalized/percent S,L) and diffing all six against cached reference output: exactly one combination scored 0 mismatches.

**Only saturation is clamped.** Channels are never clamped, so `255 128 64` reads as out-of-gamut and collapses to `159.5 159.5 159.5`, and `-0.5 0.2 0.3` prints negative. Saturation uses two one-sided comparisons, not `clamp` — that's what makes an infinity clamp to `1` while a `NaN` passes through, matching the `-nan` output for infinite input.

**`std::max`/`std::min` keep the first argument on `NaN`.** My initial `if r > g { r } else { g }` agreed for all finite input but returned `0.6 0.6 0.6` where C++ gave `nan nan nan`.

**`stof`'s `ERANGE` is judged pre-rounding.** `1.1754943e-38` is a range error but `1.17549435e-38` isn't, though both round to the same float. Rather than guess, I wrote a C probe against `strtof` to read `errno` directly, which showed the test is on the value rounded to 24 bits with an unbounded exponent. That reduces to a comparison against `2^-126 - 2^-151`.

## Verification

14 000 generated inputs byte-identical, covering equal-channel ties, the `l > 0.5` and hue-sector branches, both clamps, and `%e`/`%f` style switches. Plus every argument count, `nan`/`inf`/`-nan` in all four positions, and the error paths with matching exit code 134 and stderr text. 9 unit tests pass; both build paths compile warning-free with no dependencies.

Two caveats worth flagging:
- The 5 documented examples were far too weak to pin this down — all 5 pass against a naive `f64` mean-luminance implementation that's wrong nearly everywhere else. The fuzzing is what established correctness.
- `test9.rs` pulls modules in via `#[path]` rather than through the lib target, because requirement 7 asks for `rustc test9.rs` to work while requirement 5 asks for modules. Cargo consequently compiles the modules twice (once for the lib, once for the bin) — harmless, but it's why the declarations look unusual.
